rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 and Figures 3-9 report the authors' own development of a compact 405 nm fluorescence LIDAR mounted on a DJI Matrice 200 quadcopter and their own field measurements over a ~50 m x 100 m maize plot near Semenovskoe (Moscow region) on 24 June, 17 August and 27 September, producing fluorescence maps of the 680/740 nm band ratio.
rows.notes: The technology matches (UAV-mounted LiDAR), but the study only demonstrates feasibility of mapping a chlorophyll fluorescence ratio over a maize field and locating spots that may indicate plant stress (Figures 7 and 9; Conclusions). It reports no result of its own on productivity, yield, resource-use efficiency or sustainability; the statement that fast detection of stress changes would allow prevention of crop losses is an assertion, not a measured outcome. Detection/location of stressed plants is at most a precondition of the claimed productivity and efficiency gains, so Q2 is 'no' and upstream is set. Ancillary observations not counted for the claim: 10 parallel measurements shown as shaded reproducibility bands (Figure 5); sunlight background required flights 1-2 h before sunset; no ground-truth chlorophyll or yield validation; single field, single crop, one season.

notes: Short communication (Photonics 2022, 9, 963). Full text available; some pages duplicated/garbled by PDF extraction but all sections readable. No tables; figures are instrument photos, spectra and fluorescence maps. Data availability stated as not applicable.
